extracted.subtask_description: Judicial standards and legal criteria for assessing the Environmental Protection Agency's authority under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act (especially the scope of the 'best system of emission reduction' for existing sources) and related justiciability doctrines. Focus is on when agency rulemaking (e.g., generation-shifting limits) exceeds statutory authority and when courts require clear congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 42 U.S.C. §7411(a)(1), EPA must determine the 'best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost of achieving such reduction and any nonair quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the [Administrator] determines has been adequately demonstrated,' and then set a standard that 'reflects the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application' of that system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three-step statutory process: (1) determine the BSER (considering cost, health, non-air environmental impacts, and energy requirements); (2) ascertain the degree of emission limitation achievable through application of that system; (3) impose a performance standard reflecting that amount. EPA conducts this pollutant-by-pollutant, and for existing sources the States implement rules to meet EPA's determined level. (Text and examples: 42 U.S.C. §7411(a)(1); discussion of BSER selection and translation into emission limits.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 111(d) as a 'gap-filler' and its triggering conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111(d) operates as a 'gap-filler' authorizing EPA to regulate pollutants from existing sources only when those pollutants are not regulated under the NAAQS or the HAP (Section 112) programs and after EPA has set new-source standards under §111(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may address emissions from existing sources via §111(d) only for pollutants not covered by the other two major Clean Air Act programs (NAAQS or HAP). Historically, EPA has used §111(d) only rarely. For existing sources, EPA determines the BSER and the States submit implementation plans containing the emissions restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facility-level applicability of BSER (facility-implementable measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: When identifying a 'system of emission reduction' under Section 111, measures that can be 'put into operation at a building, structure, facility, or installation'—i.e., controls or changes that can be applied at the individual source—fit squarely within the agency's traditional §111 practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasized that prior EPA §111 rules set standards based on measures that make individual sources operate more cleanly (add-on controls, design/operation changes). The 2019 EPA interpretation limited BSER to such facility-applicable systems; generation-shifting that restructures the grid was treated as outside that traditional scope. Historical consistency with facility-level application weighs against novel grid-level interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine / clear congressional authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency claims authority to make decisions of vast 'economic and political significance'—transformative powers that effectively restructure major sectors—the major questions doctrine requires a clear statement from Congress authorizing that authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 'extraordinary cases' where the asserted agency power is historically unprecedented or would have vast economic/political significance, courts must hesitate and demand clear congressional authorization (Brown & Williamson; Utility Air; Gonzales; NFIB examples cited). The agency's vague statutory grant (e.g., the word 'system' in §111) is insufficient without a clear indication Congress intended such breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical agency practice and precedent in statutory interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Longstanding agency practice and historical usage of a statutory provision inform a court's view of what Congress intended and counsel skepticism toward suddenly novel or expansive readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court noted that for four decades EPA consistently interpreted §111 to require source-applied measures; that history supports reading 'system of emission reduction' to refer to measures applicable to individual sources. Prior usage is an important (though not necessarily dispositive) interpretive factor when an agency claims new expansive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justiciability: standing to appeal — 'fairly traceable' injury and redress
rubrics_metrics.description: In appeals assessing standing, the appellant must show an injury 'fairly traceable to the judgment below' and that a favorable ruling would redress that injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to petitions for review: vacatur that purports to bring a prior rule back into legal effect can inflict regulatory injury (e.g., requiring more stringent regulation within a State). The Court distinguished mootness from standing and required the Government to prove mootness when asserting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mootness and voluntary cessation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary cessation of challenged behavior by the Government does not moot a case unless it is 'absolutely clear' that the allegedly wrongful behavior cannot reasonably be expected to recur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Government represents it will not enforce a rule pending new rulemaking, courts will not treat the case as moot unless the Government carries the heavy burden of showing future recurrence is impossible. (Citing Parents Involved and other precedent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of BSER into emissions limits must be tethered to feasible, source-applicable measures
rubrics_metrics.description: In translating a chosen BSER into operational numerical performance rates, EPA must base its stringency choices on feasible applications of that system—modeling of what is achievable without imposing measures that can only be met via sector-wide restructuring beyond source-level application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may select the degree of stringency but must ground that choice in modeling of how much cleaner generation natural gas and renewables can supply without undue costs or reliability problems. The Court rejected setting emission ceilings so strict that no existing source could comply absent sector-wide generation shifting beyond facility-level measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of cost, grid reliability, and energy impacts in BSER and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining BSER and the degree of emission limitation achievable, EPA must take into account cost, health, non-air environmental impacts, and energy requirements (including grid reliability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory text requires consideration of cost and energy impacts. The Court noted EPA's modeling of projected costs, retirements, price increases, and reliability effects as part of its determination of feasible generation shifts; such considerations factor into whether proposed measures are within statutory authority and feasible to implement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on relying on other Clean Air Act programs to justify broader §111 authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to other Clean Air Act programs (e.g., Acid Rain, NAAQS) that use 'systems' or sector-wide mechanisms does not by itself supply the clear congressional authorization to read §111(d) as permitting grid-level generation shifting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court explained that because other programs may use 'systems' in different ways, the mere fact that sector-wide trading or systems occur under other provisions does not transform the meaning of 'system of emission reduction' in §111 into a clear delegation to restructure an entire sector without a clear congressional statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of States in §111(d) implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: For existing sources, States (not EPA directly) set the actual enforceable rules governing sources in their borders after EPA determines the BSER and the emission limitation to be achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA determines the permissible level of pollution reduction (the amount to be achieved); States submit plans with the emissions restrictions they will adopt and enforce so sources within the State meet EPA's determined level. This federal-state implementation flow is central to §111(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of cap-and-trade or trading mechanisms under §111
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of market mechanisms (cap-and-trade, allowance trading) is not categorically impossible under §111, but courts examine whether the emissions cap and scheme are rooted in plant- or source-specific achievable technologies/measures or instead depend on sector-wide generation shifting beyond source-level application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court contrasted the 2005 Mercury Rule (which allowed trading but set the cap based on technologies installable nationwide) with the Clean Power Plan (which produced caps that could not be met by plant-level measures alone). Whether trading is used, and how the numerical cap was determined, affects whether the approach conforms to §111.
